cards.definition: A time series is a collection of observations indexed by time. The ordering and spacing of observations carry information, so treating the values as an unordered independent sample can discard essential structure.
major_error_concepts: Discarding time order while claiming to preserve all time-series information.
cards.prompt: What is Time Series? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Observations indexed by time.
Order and spacing matter.

accepted_variants: A probability model for random trajectories.
cards.definition: A stochastic process is a family of random variables indexed by time or another index. An observed time series is one realization of the process, not the entire collection of possible paths.
major_error_concepts: Equating one observed trajectory with the full probability law.
cards.prompt: What is Stochastic Process? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Family of indexed random variables.
Observed path differs from process law.

cards.definition: The sampling interval is the elapsed time between consecutive observations. For equally spaced observations it is constant; irregular intervals require methods that account for the actual time gaps.
major_error_concepts: Treating unequal time gaps as equal without changing the interpretation of lags.
cards.prompt: What is Sampling Interval? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Elapsed time between observations.
Equal spacing is an assumption, not automatic.

cards.definition: A lag of k compares a time-series value with a value k observation steps earlier. In regularly sampled data its elapsed duration is k times the sampling interval.
major_error_concepts: Assuming lag one always means one day regardless of sampling cadence.
cards.prompt: What is Lag? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Displacement by observation steps.
Duration depends on sampling interval.

cards.definition: The mean function of a process is m(t)=E[X_t], when the expectation exists. It describes the ensemble average at each time and need not equal the average along one observed path.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the mean function must be constant for every process.
cards.prompt: What is Mean Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Expected value at each time.
Ensemble mean is not automatically a path average.

cards.definition: The autocovariance function is Cov(X_t,X_s) when the second moments exist. It describes linear dependence across times; for a weakly stationary process it depends only on the lag t-s.
major_error_concepts: Treating zero autocovariance as proof of independence in general.
cards.prompt: What is Autocovariance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Covariance between values at different times.
Lag-only form requires stationarity.

accepted_variants: The correlation of a series with its lagged values.
cards.definition: Autocorrelation is covariance at a lag divided by the relevant standard deviations. For a weakly stationary process with positive variance, rho(k)=gamma(k)/gamma(0), so rho(0)=1.
major_error_concepts: Using unnormalized covariance as a correlation coefficient.
cards.prompt: What is Autocorrelation Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Normalized lagged covariance.
Positive variance required.

cards.definition: Strict stationarity means every finite-dimensional joint distribution is unchanged by a common shift of all time indices. It concerns the entire distribution, not only a constant mean or variance.
major_error_concepts: Concluding strict stationarity solely from a flat observed mean.
cards.prompt: What is Strict Stationarity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: All finite-dimensional laws are shift-invariant.

cards.definition: Weak stationarity requires finite second moments, a constant mean, and autocovariance depending only on lag. It is a second-order condition and does not generally imply strict stationarity.
major_error_concepts: Calling any constant-mean process weakly stationary despite changing variance.
cards.prompt: What is Weak Stationarity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Constant mean and lag-only covariance with finite second moments.

accepted_variants: A process with multivariate normal finite-dimensional distributions.
cards.definition: A Gaussian process has jointly Gaussian values for every finite set of times. Its finite-dimensional laws are determined by means and covariances, so weak stationarity implies strict stationarity for such a process.
major_error_concepts: Assuming Gaussian one-time marginals alone guarantee joint Gaussianity.
cards.prompt: What is Gaussian Process? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Every finite vector is jointly Gaussian.
Mean and covariance determine its laws.

cards.definition: White noise has zero mean, constant finite variance, and zero covariance at every nonzero lag. Without an additional assumption it need not be independent or Gaussian.
major_error_concepts: Claiming all white noise consists of independent normal observations.
cards.prompt: What is White Noise? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Zero mean, constant variance, zero nonzero-lag covariance.
Uncorrelated need not mean independent.

accepted_variants: IID innovations when used as a model input.
cards.definition: Independent identically distributed noise consists of mutually independent variables sharing one distribution. With zero mean and finite variance it is white noise, but second-order white noise alone is weaker.
major_error_concepts: Inferring independence merely from a zero sample autocorrelation.
cards.prompt: What is IID Noise? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Independence and identical laws.
White-noise conditions alone are insufficient.

cards.definition: An innovation is the part of X_t left after predicting it from past information. For conditional-mean prediction it has conditional mean zero given that past, though it need not have constant variance or be independent over time.
major_error_concepts: Defining innovations without specifying the information used for prediction.
cards.prompt: What is Innovation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: New prediction error relative to the specified past.
Conditional mean zero for conditional-mean innovations.

cards.definition: Ergodicity permits suitable averages along one long stationary trajectory to recover corresponding population expectations. Stationarity alone does not ensure this identification; a process can retain random path-specific features forever.
major_error_concepts: Treating every dependent stationary sample as IID or automatically ergodic.
cards.prompt: What is Ergodicity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Path averages recover ensemble quantities under ergodic assumptions.
Stationarity alone is insufficient.

cards.definition: Stationary increments means the distribution of X_(t+h)-X_t depends on h but not on the starting time t. A process can have stationary increments while its levels are nonstationary.
major_error_concepts: Calling a random walk stationary merely because its increments are stationary.
cards.prompt: What is Stationary Increments? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Increment laws depend on duration, not starting time.
Does not imply stationary levels.

accepted_variants: A fixed function of time in the mean.
cards.definition: A deterministic trend is a nonrandom systematic component of a series that varies with time, such as a linear trend. Removing a correctly specified deterministic trend can leave a stationary remainder.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every persistent trend is deterministic.
cards.prompt: What is Deterministic Trend? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Nonrandom time-varying systematic component.

cards.definition: Seasonality is recurring structure associated with a known calendar or fixed observation period. Its period is tied to the sampling schedule, unlike cycles whose durations may vary.
major_error_concepts: Calling any slow fluctuation seasonal without a stable period.
cards.prompt: What is Seasonality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Recurring structure at a specified regular period.

accepted_variants: Recurring but not strictly periodic movement.
cards.definition: A cycle is an oscillatory pattern that need not have a fixed duration or calendar alignment. A cyclic component may vary in amplitude and period, so it is not necessarily seasonal.
major_error_concepts: Equating every cycle with fixed seasonal repetition.
cards.prompt: What is Cyclic Component? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Oscillation without necessarily fixed calendar period.

cards.definition: Additive decomposition expresses an observation as trend plus seasonal component plus remainder. It suits seasonal fluctuations whose absolute size is roughly stable across the series level.
major_error_concepts: Claiming additive seasonality necessarily scales proportionally with the level.
cards.prompt: What is Additive Decomposition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Sum of components.
Roughly level-independent seasonal amplitude.

cards.definition: Multiplicative decomposition expresses positive observations as a product of trend, seasonal factor, and remainder factor. A logarithm converts that product into a sum when the components are positive.
major_error_concepts: Applying a real logarithm directly to nonpositive observations.
cards.prompt: What is Multiplicative Decomposition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Product of positive components.
Logarithms yield additive components.

cards.definition: Detrending removes an estimated deterministic time component. It differs from differencing, which transforms consecutive observations and can remove stochastic trends as well as deterministic ones.
major_error_concepts: Assuming detrending always eliminates a unit-root stochastic trend.
cards.prompt: What is Detrending? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Remove a modeled deterministic trend.
Distinct from differencing.

cards.definition: The backshift operator B maps X_t to X_(t-1), and B^k shifts it k observations backward. Lag polynomials compactly express linear time-series models.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting B as moving an observation forward in time.
cards.prompt: What is Backshift Operator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.

cards.definition: First differencing forms Delta X_t=X_t-X_(t-1)=(1-B)X_t. It measures consecutive change and can remove one unit root, but need not make an arbitrary process stationary.
major_error_concepts: Claiming one difference always yields stationarity.
cards.prompt: What is First Difference? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Current value minus its immediate predecessor.
Stationarity is not guaranteed.

cards.definition: Seasonal differencing forms X_t-X_(t-s) for seasonal period s. It compares matching seasonal positions and is distinct from an ordinary first difference when s is greater than one.
major_error_concepts: Subtracting the previous observation and calling it an annual seasonal difference for monthly data.
cards.prompt: What is Seasonal Difference? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Difference separated by seasonal period s.

cards.definition: Overdifferencing applies more differencing than the process needs. It can add avoidable noise or induce a moving-average unit-root structure, degrading forecasts rather than improving stationarity.
major_error_concepts: Assuming additional differences always improve the model.
cards.prompt: What is Overdifferencing? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Unnecessary differencing can distort dependence and increase noise.

cards.definition: A sample autocorrelation estimates a lag correlation from one finite observed series. Its uncertainty depends on dependence and model assumptions, so individual spikes are not definitive evidence of a specific process.
major_error_concepts: Treating every nonzero sample ACF value as a true dependence.
cards.prompt: What is Sample Autocorrelation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Finite-sample estimate of lag correlation.
Sampling variability matters.

accepted_variants: The final-lag coefficient in an appropriate lag regression.
cards.definition: Partial autocorrelation at lag k measures linear association between X_t and X_(t-k) after accounting for the intermediate lags. It isolates the incremental linear contribution of that lag, not a general causal effect.
major_error_concepts: Calling the ordinary ACF the PACF without removing intermediate-lag effects.
cards.prompt: What is Partial Autocorrelation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Lag correlation adjusted for intermediate lags.
Linear association, not causation.

cards.definition: An AR(1) process obeys X_t=c+phi X_(t-1)+epsilon_t. A causal stationary solution with finite-variance white-noise input exists when |phi|<1, with mean c/(1-phi).
major_error_concepts: Claiming phi=1 gives the same stationary model as |phi|<1.
cards.prompt: What is AR(1) Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Current value depends linearly on previous value and noise.
Causal stationarity requires |phi|<1.

cards.definition: For the causal stationary solution of X_t=c+phi X_(t-1)+epsilon_t with |phi|<1 and white-noise variance sigma^2>0, mu=c/(1-phi), gamma(k)=sigma^2 phi^|k|/(1-phi^2), and rho(k)=phi^|k|. The causal stable assumption is part of the formula: a merely stationary noncausal solution is not covered. At |phi|=1 these covariance expressions do not define this nondegenerate stationary model.
major_error_concepts: For phi=2 and sigma^2=1, every stationary AR(1) has variance 1/(1-4)=-1/3.
cards.prompt: Give the autocovariance and autocorrelation of a causal stationary AR(1), including the assumptions required for these formulas.
required_concepts: Use the causal stable regime |phi|<1 with positive finite white-noise variance.
State gamma(k)=sigma^2 phi^|k|/(1-phi^2) and rho(k)=phi^|k|.

cards.definition: An AR(p) model regresses a value on its previous p values plus an intercept and noise. Its order counts included consecutive lags, not the length of the observed series.
major_error_concepts: Defining p as the number of observations in the dataset.
cards.prompt: What is Autoregressive Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Linear dependence on p past values plus noise.

cards.definition: For the polynomial phi(z)=1-phi_1 z-...-phi_p z^p, a causal stationary AR process requires all roots outside the unit circle. The condition concerns the polynomial roots, not each coefficient separately.
major_error_concepts: Checking only that every coefficient has magnitude less than one and declaring stability.
cards.prompt: What is Autoregressive Root Condition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Roots of the stated AR polynomial lie outside |z|=1.

cards.definition: A causal linear process represents the present using current and past noise terms with suitably summable coefficients. It does not require future noise to construct the current value.
major_error_concepts: Confusing causal representation with proof of real-world causal effects.
cards.prompt: What is Causal Time-Series Representation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Dependence on present and past, not future, noise.

cards.definition: An MA(1) process has X_t=mu+epsilon_t+theta epsilon_(t-1) for white noise epsilon. It is weakly stationary for any finite theta under finite noise variance; invertibility is a separate condition.
major_error_concepts: Claiming MA(1) stationarity requires |theta|<1.
cards.prompt: What is MA(1) Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Current plus one lagged noise term.
Stationarity distinct from invertibility.

cards.definition: An MA(q) model is a finite linear combination of current and q previous white-noise inputs plus a mean. Its autocovariance is zero beyond lag q, assuming the usual white-noise input.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting MA(q) as a rolling average of the observed values rather than a model of noise inputs.
cards.prompt: What is Moving-Average Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Finite sum of lagged noise.
Population covariance cuts off after q.

cards.definition: Invertibility permits the driving noise to be recovered from current and past observations through a stable linear filter. With theta(z)=1+theta_1 z+...+theta_q z^q, the standard MA condition places all roots outside the unit circle.
major_error_concepts: Treating invertibility and stationarity as the same condition.
cards.prompt: What is Invertibility? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Stable recovery of noise from observed history.
Roots outside unit circle for the stated polynomial.

cards.definition: A centered ARMA(p,q) representation is phi(B)(X_t-mu)=theta(B)epsilon_t, where phi(z)=1-sum_(j=1)^p phi_j z^j and theta(z)=1+sum_(j=1)^q theta_j z^j, and epsilon is white noise. For a reduced representation with no common polynomial factors and positive noise variance, roots of phi outside the unit circle give the stable causal solution; roots of theta outside it give invertibility. Redundant common factors must be recognized before using these root tests to classify the representation or its order.
major_error_concepts: Since X_t=epsilon_t also satisfies (1-B)X_t=(1-B)epsilon_t, the uncancelled root at one proves this white-noise process is nonstationary.
cards.prompt: Define an ARMA model and explain the reduced-representation convention for its causal and invertibility root tests.
required_concepts: Combine AR and MA lag-polynomial terms with a consistent sign convention.
State separate AR causality and MA invertibility conditions.
Use a reduced representation for interpreting the usual root tests and orders.

cards.definition: For a pure stationary AR(p), the population PACF cuts off after p while the ACF typically decays. For a pure MA(q), the population ACF cuts off after q while the PACF typically decays; sample plots only approximate these patterns.
major_error_concepts: Treating the patterns as exact rules for noisy sample plots or arbitrary mixed models.
cards.prompt: What is ACF and PACF Model Identification? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: AR PACF cutoff and MA ACF cutoff.
Finite-sample plots are uncertain.

cards.definition: For a centered causal stationary AR(p), X_t=sum_(j=1)^p phi_j X_(t-j)+epsilon_t, with white-noise innovation variance sigma^2, gamma(k)=sum_(j=1)^p phi_j gamma(k-j) for k≥1, and gamma(0)=sum_(j=1)^p phi_j gamma(j)+sigma^2. Here gamma(-k)=gamma(k). The first p positive-lag equations form Gamma_p phi=(gamma(1),...,gamma(p))^T with entries (Gamma_p)_(i,j)=gamma(i-j). Replacing population covariances by estimates gives Yule-Walker estimation.
major_error_concepts: Yule-Walker gives gamma(0)=sum_j phi_j gamma(j), with no innovation variance term.
cards.prompt: State the positive-lag and zero-lag Yule-Walker equations for a causal stationary AR(p).
required_concepts: State the positive-lag autocovariance recursion for a causal stationary AR model.
Include the innovation variance in the zero-lag equation.
If a matrix form is used, its Toeplitz entries must agree with gamma(i-j); a separate matrix restatement is not required.

cards.definition: Conditional least squares estimates time-series parameters by minimizing squared prediction errors conditional on chosen starting values. Its treatment of initial observations can differ from an exact likelihood calculation.
major_error_concepts: Claiming conditional least squares and exact likelihood always coincide.
cards.prompt: What is Conditional Least Squares? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Minimize squared conditional errors.
Initial-value conditioning matters.

accepted_variants: Likelihood based on model-implied covariance or sequential innovations.
cards.definition: A Gaussian time-series likelihood uses the joint normal law implied by the model, including dependence across observations. Multiplying marginal normal densities as if observations were independent generally gives a different likelihood.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring off-diagonal dependence while claiming an exact correlated Gaussian likelihood.
cards.prompt: What is Gaussian Time-Series Likelihood? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Joint Gaussian law includes serial covariance.

cards.definition: A forecast origin is the final time whose observations are available when a prediction is issued. Every input and fitted transformation must respect that information cutoff.
major_error_concepts: Allowing later measurements into an earlier-origin prediction.
cards.prompt: What is Forecast Origin? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Last available information time.
No future observations at the origin.

cards.definition: A forecast horizon is the time distance from the forecast origin to the target observation. One-step and many-step forecasts can have different errors and require distinct evaluation.
major_error_concepts: Equating the forecast horizon with training sample length.
cards.prompt: What is Forecast Horizon? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Distance from origin to target.

cards.definition: Under squared-error loss, the optimal point forecast is the conditional mean of the future target given available information, provided the required moments exist. Other loss functions can imply different optimal summaries.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the conditional mean is optimal under every loss.
cards.prompt: What is Conditional-Mean Forecast? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Conditional mean minimizes expected squared loss.
Information set and loss must be specified.

cards.definition: For a stationary AR(1), the h-step conditional-mean forecast is mu+phi^h(X_t-mu), assuming future innovations have conditional mean zero. It reverts toward mu as h grows when |phi|<1.
major_error_concepts: Predicting linear growth forever from a stable zero-trend AR(1).
cards.prompt: What is AR(1) Multi-Step Forecast? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Geometric decay of deviation from stationary mean.

cards.definition: Forecast error is the realized target minus the forecast made from the stated origin. Its variance generally changes with horizon and should not be confused with uncertainty in an estimated mean alone.
major_error_concepts: Equating all forecast-error variance with parameter-estimation variance.
cards.prompt: What is Forecast Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Future realization minus issued forecast.
Horizon-specific uncertainty.

cards.definition: A prediction interval is intended to cover a future observation with a specified probability under stated assumptions. It includes future observation uncertainty and is generally wider than an interval for a mean forecast alone.
major_error_concepts: Using a mean confidence interval as though it covered individual future outcomes at the same level.
cards.prompt: What is Prediction Interval? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Interval for a future outcome.
Includes future noise.

cards.definition: The naive h-step forecast is Xhat_(t+h|t)=X_t. It is the conditional-mean forecast for a driftless process whose future increments have conditional mean zero given the available filtration, with the required finite moments; a martingale with finite second moments is a sufficient setting. Merely zero unconditional increment means are not enough. As a practical last-value baseline it can still be used without claiming optimality.
major_error_concepts: If every increment has unconditional mean zero, the last observation is always the optimal forecast even when the next increment is predictable from the past.
cards.prompt: Define the naive forecast and state a sufficient conditional-information assumption for its squared-error optimality.
required_concepts: Define the last-observation forecast.
Conditional-mean optimality requires zero conditional expected future increments, not only zero unconditional means.
Distinguish use as a baseline from proof of optimality.

cards.definition: A seasonal naive forecast repeats the last observed value from the corresponding seasonal position. It uses the established seasonal period and provides a baseline for series with recurring seasonal patterns.
major_error_concepts: Using the immediately previous period regardless of seasonal alignment.
cards.prompt: What is Seasonal Naive Forecast? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Repeat the latest matching seasonal position.

cards.definition: A recursive multi-step forecast repeatedly applies a one-step model, substituting earlier forecasts where future lagged values are unavailable. Errors and uncertainty propagate across these substitutions.
major_error_concepts: Substituting actual future lag values that were unavailable at the forecast origin.
cards.prompt: What is Recursive Forecasting? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Iterate one-step predictions using predicted lag values.

cards.definition: A direct multi-step forecast fits a separate relationship for a chosen horizon instead of iterating only a one-step model. It can avoid some recursive error propagation but requires horizon-specific estimation.
major_error_concepts: Calling repeated one-step substitution a direct forecast.
cards.prompt: What is Direct Forecasting? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Estimate horizon-specific prediction directly.

cards.definition: A standard finite-variance driftless random walk starts at fixed X_0 and has X_t=X_0+sum_(j=1)^t epsilon_j with iid increments of mean zero and variance 0<sigma^2<infinity. Then E[X_t]=X_0 and Var(X_t)=t sigma^2, so its levels are not weakly stationary even though its increments are stationary. The variance identity also holds under the weaker assumption of pairwise uncorrelated, common-variance increments; independence is not needed for that calculation alone.
major_error_concepts: Even with epsilon_t identically zero, a fixed-start random walk has variance t and cannot be stationary.
cards.prompt: State a basic finite-variance driftless random-walk model and derive why its levels are not weakly stationary.
required_concepts: Represent levels as accumulated increments from a fixed start.
State positive finite common increment variance and independence or sufficient uncorrelatedness for the variance calculation.
Variance t sigma^2 changes with time, unlike the increment variance.

cards.definition: A random walk with drift adds a constant expected increment: X_t=d+X_(t-1)+epsilon_t. Its mean trajectory grows linearly while its stochastic shocks still accumulate rather than decay.
major_error_concepts: Treating removal of the deterministic drift as removing the stochastic unit root.
cards.prompt: What is Random Walk with Drift? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Constant mean increment plus accumulated shocks.

accepted_variants: Nonstable persistence at a unit-modulus root.
cards.definition: A unit root is a root on the unit circle in the autoregressive lag polynomial. A root at one produces a stochastic trend that ordinary differencing can remove under suitable model assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Calling a large but strictly stable AR coefficient exactly a unit root.
cards.prompt: What is Unit Root? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: AR polynomial root on the unit circle.
Root one motivates ordinary differencing.

cards.definition: An I(d) process becomes stationary after d ordinary differences, with d the minimum such number under the model. The designation concerns integration order, not the autoregressive order p.
major_error_concepts: Equating integration order with number of AR lags.
cards.prompt: What is Order of Integration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Minimum differences required for stationarity.

cards.definition: A trend-stationary process is stationary after removing a deterministic trend. A difference-stationary process instead needs differencing to remove its stochastic trend; using the wrong transformation can leave or introduce dependence problems.
major_error_concepts: Treating detrending and differencing as interchangeable for every process.
cards.prompt: What is Trend and Difference Stationarity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Detrending versus differencing remove different trend types.

cards.definition: An ARIMA(p,d,q) model applies an ARMA(p,q) model to a series after d ordinary differences. Its forecasts for levels must reverse the differencing and accumulate the corresponding uncertainty.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting differenced predictions directly as predicted levels.
cards.prompt: What is ARIMA Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: ARMA for differenced series.
Return forecasts to the original level scale.

cards.definition: A seasonal ARIMA model adds seasonal autoregressive, differencing, and moving-average operators at period s to ordinary ARIMA terms. Seasonal and nonseasonal orders describe different lag structures.
major_error_concepts: Omitting the seasonal period while claiming the seasonal orders fully specify the model.
cards.prompt: What is Seasonal ARIMA Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Seasonal lag-polynomial terms with explicit period s.

cards.definition: A deterministic seasonal regression represents recurring seasonal means using fixed indicators or periodic basis functions. It models predictable mean variation rather than necessarily imposing a seasonal unit root.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every seasonal pattern must be seasonally differenced.
cards.prompt: What is Seasonal Regression? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Fixed seasonal mean terms.
Distinct from seasonal differencing.

cards.definition: An augmented Dickey-Fuller test assesses a unit-root null using a regression with lagged differences and chosen deterministic terms. Its reference distribution is nonstandard; failure to reject does not prove a unit root.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting failure to reject as proof of stationarity.
cards.prompt: What is Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Null hypothesis is a unit root.
Deterministic terms and lag choice affect interpretation.

cards.definition: A stationarity-null test takes level or trend stationarity as the null, depending on the specification. Rejection challenges that stationarity model; it does not alone identify a unique alternative process.
major_error_concepts: Treating all stationarity tests as having a unit-root null.
cards.prompt: What is Stationarity-Null Test? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Stationarity is the null.
Specification determines level versus trend interpretation.

cards.definition: An estimated residual is the observed value minus a fitted or predicted value under an estimated model. Residuals approximate innovations but also reflect parameter fitting, model error, and initial-condition choices.
major_error_concepts: Assuming fitted residuals are automatically IID because the model labels its errors IID.
cards.prompt: What is Time-Series Residual? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Observed-minus-fitted difference.
Not identical to true latent innovations.

cards.definition: A weak-white-noise residual process has mean zero, constant finite variance, and zero autocovariance at every nonzero lag. Fitted sample residuals can be checked for departures, but a nonsignificant diagnostic at a finite set of lags does not establish population whiteness. Even true zero autocovariance does not establish independence or constant conditional variance; nonlinear dependence can remain.
major_error_concepts: A nonsignificant autocorrelation test proves the residuals are independent with constant conditional variance.
cards.prompt: Distinguish residual whiteness from failure to detect sample autocorrelation, and state what whiteness does not imply.
required_concepts: Whiteness is a process property: zero mean, constant finite variance, zero nonzero-lag autocovariances.
Not detecting correlation in a finite sample is weaker than proving that property.
Uncorrelatedness does not exclude nonlinear dependence or conditional heteroskedasticity.

cards.definition: For n residuals and lag limit h<n, the Ljung-Box statistic is Q=n(n+2)sum_(k=1)^h rhat_k^2/(n-k). It combines evidence against zero residual autocorrelations at those lags. For suitably fitted regular ARMA(p,q) models under the usual innovation assumptions, a common large-sample approximation compares Q to chi-square with h-p-q degrees of freedom, requiring h>p+q. This calibration is approximate and model-dependent; nonrejection is not proof of whiteness at every lag or of an entirely correct model.
major_error_concepts: For residuals from any fitted ARMA(p,q), compare the unscaled sum of autocorrelations to chi-square with n degrees of freedom; nonrejection proves independence.
cards.prompt: Give the Ljung-Box portmanteau statistic and its usual approximate calibration for fitted ARMA residuals.
required_concepts: Give the Ljung-Box statistic with its n(n+2), squared autocorrelation, and n-k factors.
Specify the tested lag limit and account for ARMA parameter fitting in the usual approximate degrees of freedom.
Interpret nonrejection as limited evidence, not model certification.

cards.definition: AIC balances maximized log likelihood against model complexity using a penalty of twice the number of estimated parameters. It compares candidate predictive models on a compatible likelihood and data basis, not arbitrary unrelated scores.
major_error_concepts: Comparing AIC values from incompatible response data as though they were directly comparable.
cards.prompt: What is Akaike Information Criterion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Minus twice log likelihood plus 2k.
Comparable fitted data and likelihood needed.

cards.definition: BIC penalizes maximized log likelihood using k log n, where k is parameter count and n is sample size. It uses a different complexity penalty and motivation from AIC and need not select the same model.
major_error_concepts: Claiming BIC always makes the same selection as AIC.
cards.prompt: What is Bayesian Information Criterion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Minus twice log likelihood plus k log n.

cards.definition: Chronological holdout reserves later observations for evaluation after fitting on earlier observations. It preserves the direction of information flow and should reflect the intended forecast horizon and operating conditions.
major_error_concepts: Randomly mixing future observations into training for an earlier-origin forecasting claim.
cards.prompt: What is Chronological Holdout? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Earlier training and later evaluation.
Respect prediction timing.

cards.definition: Rolling-origin evaluation repeatedly advances the forecast origin and records forecasts made using only information available at each origin. It measures performance across multiple historical prediction opportunities.
major_error_concepts: Fitting preprocessing to the entire series before evaluating all past origins.
cards.prompt: What is Rolling-Origin Evaluation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Repeated time-ordered forecasting from advancing origins.

cards.definition: An expanding training window retains all earlier observations as the origin advances. A sliding window keeps only a chosen recent span, trading reduced historical information for greater responsiveness to change.
major_error_concepts: Calling a fixed recent window an expanding window.
cards.prompt: What is Training-Window Choice? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: All accumulated history versus fixed recent span.

cards.definition: Forecast leakage occurs when prediction or model selection uses information unavailable at the claimed forecast origin. Examples include future-derived scaling, revised data unavailable then, and centered smoothers crossing the cutoff.
major_error_concepts: Assuming preprocessing cannot leak because it does not use the prediction target explicitly.
cards.prompt: What is Forecast Leakage? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Unavailable future information contaminates evaluation.

cards.definition: Mean absolute error averages absolute forecast errors on the target scale. It emphasizes the magnitude of typical misses without squaring them and is optimized by a conditional median under absolute-error loss.
major_error_concepts: Claiming squared-error and absolute-error loss always imply the same optimal forecast.
cards.prompt: What is Mean Absolute Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Average absolute errors.
Median is the corresponding optimal point forecast.

cards.definition: Root mean squared error is the square root of average squared forecast errors. It is expressed in target units and gives large errors more influence than mean absolute error.
major_error_concepts: Taking the mean of signed errors and calling it RMSE.
cards.prompt: What is Root Mean Squared Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Square root of mean squared errors.
Greater sensitivity to large misses.

cards.definition: A scaled absolute forecast error divides absolute error by a training-sample baseline error scale, often from naive or seasonal-naive differences. The scale must be positive and specified to make comparisons interpretable.
major_error_concepts: Computing the scaling baseline from future held-out targets without disclosure.
cards.prompt: What is Scaled Forecast Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Normalize absolute error by a defined training baseline.
Zero denominator requires special handling.

cards.definition: Interval coverage is the fraction of evaluated targets falling within their issued prediction intervals. It should be assessed with interval width and relevant horizon or subgroup conditioning, because trivially broad intervals can cover often.
major_error_concepts: Calling arbitrarily wide intervals informative solely because their coverage is high.
cards.prompt: What is Forecast Interval Coverage? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Observed inclusion frequency for issued intervals.
Coverage alone does not measure sharpness.

cards.definition: Simple exponential smoothing updates a level estimate by a weighted average of the latest observation and previous level, with weight alpha between zero and one. Its basic forecast is flat and does not include an explicit trend or seasonality.
major_error_concepts: Claiming basic simple exponential smoothing explicitly extrapolates a linear trend.
cards.prompt: What is Simple Exponential Smoothing? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Recursive exponentially decaying weights.
Level-only model in its basic form.

cards.definition: Holt's method maintains separate level and trend estimates and extrapolates the estimated trend for forecasting. A damped version reduces the trend's future contribution as the horizon increases.
major_error_concepts: Treating Holt's trend method as having no trend component.
cards.prompt: What is Holt Trend Method? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Separate recursive level and trend estimates.

cards.definition: Holt-Winters methods extend level and trend smoothing with a seasonal component. Additive and multiplicative seasonal versions reflect whether seasonal magnitude is roughly absolute or proportional to level.
major_error_concepts: Using multiplicative seasonal factors without considering nonpositive values.
cards.prompt: What is Holt-Winters Method? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Level, trend, and seasonal smoothing.
Seasonal form should match scale behavior.

cards.definition: An exponential-smoothing state-space model gives smoothing recursions a probabilistic observation and state-evolution interpretation. The error, trend, and seasonal choices determine both forecasts and model-based uncertainty.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a smoothing formula alone specifies a unique forecast distribution.
cards.prompt: What is Exponential-Smoothing State-Space Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Probabilistic model for smoothing state updates.
Uncertainty depends on model specification.

cards.definition: A state-space model relates observations to latent states through an observation equation and evolves those states through a transition equation. The two equations separate measurement noise from underlying system dynamics.
major_error_concepts: Equating the unobserved state exactly with every noisy observation.
cards.prompt: What is State-Space Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Observation equation plus latent-state transition.
Separate measurement and process noise.

cards.definition: A local-level model has observations equal to a latent level plus measurement noise, while the level follows a random walk. It permits gradual level changes and distinguishes state disturbance variance from observation-noise variance.
major_error_concepts: Assuming level evolution and observation noise must have equal variances.
cards.prompt: What is Local-Level Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Noisy observations of a random-walk level.
Two distinct noise sources.

cards.definition: The Kalman filter recursively predicts and updates state estimates and covariances in a linear state-space model. Under Gaussian assumptions it gives exact conditional state distributions; otherwise it retains a linear-estimation interpretation under suitable moments.
major_error_concepts: Claiming exact Bayesian filtering for every nonlinear non-Gaussian model.
cards.prompt: What is Kalman Filter? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Recursive prediction and measurement update.
Exact distributional interpretation needs linear Gaussian assumptions.

cards.definition: For measurement y=H x+v with zero-mean measurement noise independent of the prior state error, let the predicted state mean and covariance be m^- and P^-, with measurement-noise covariance R. If S=H P^- H^T+R is invertible, the Kalman gain is K=P^- H^T S^(-1), and m^+=m^-+K(y-Hm^-). Under the linear-Gaussian model this is the conditional-mean update. The gain weights the innovation using prediction and measurement uncertainty rather than treating the measurement as exact.
major_error_concepts: The Kalman gain is always H P^- R^(-1), even with singular R, and all measurements replace the predicted state exactly.
cards.prompt: Give the Kalman-gain formula for the independent-noise linear measurement model and explain its role in the update.
required_concepts: Define S=H P^- H^T+R and require the inverse to exist for this form.
Give K=P^- H^T S^(-1) in the correct matrix order.
The gain multiplies the measurement innovation in the state-mean update.

cards.definition: Filtering estimates a state using observations only through that time. Smoothing estimates a past state using later observations as well, so a smoothed historical estimate is not an honest real-time filtered estimate.
major_error_concepts: Using a future-informed smoothed state as an available real-time predictor.
cards.prompt: What is Filtering and Smoothing? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Filtering uses past and present; smoothing can use future data.

cards.definition: When a state-space observation is missing and the missingness mechanism is ignorable for the state inference, propagate the prediction but skip that absent measurement update. In a partially observed measurement vector, update using the observed components and their corresponding model matrices/covariance. Missing does not mean observed zero. If missingness depends informatively on the latent state or unseen measurement, its indicator may supply likelihood information and must be modeled instead of automatically ignored.
major_error_concepts: Even if a sensor systematically fails only at extreme latent states, a missing record is always information-free and should be treated as an observed zero.
cards.prompt: How are missing observations handled in state-space filtering, and when is simply skipping an update unjustified?
required_concepts: Predict across the gap and omit only the unavailable, ignorable measurement contribution.
Use observed components when a measurement vector is partially available.
A missingness mechanism that carries latent-state information cannot automatically be discarded.

cards.definition: Serially correlated regression errors violate the usual independent-error covariance formula. Depending on regressor exogeneity, coefficient estimates may remain consistent while conventional standard errors become misleading.
major_error_concepts: Claiming serial correlation always leaves both estimates and conventional standard errors unaffected.
cards.prompt: What is Serial Correlation in Regression? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Serial dependence changes inference.
Coefficient validity also depends on exogeneity.

cards.definition: A heteroskedasticity-and-autocorrelation-consistent covariance estimator adjusts regression uncertainty for specified forms of dependent, unequal-variance errors under regularity conditions. It does not repair endogeneity or an incorrect conditional mean model.
major_error_concepts: Claiming robust standard errors make biased causal coefficients valid.
cards.prompt: What is HAC Standard Errors? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Robust covariance for heteroskedastic and serial dependence.
Not a cure for endogeneity.

cards.definition: A distributed-lag model includes current or past predictor values to represent delayed associations with a response. Interpreting its coefficients requires the chosen lag structure and suitable assumptions about predictor exogeneity.
major_error_concepts: Declaring lagged association automatically causal.
cards.prompt: What is Distributed-Lag Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Response depends on several timed predictor values.
Causal interpretation needs additional assumptions.

cards.definition: A vector autoregression models each component of a multivariate series using lags of all included components. It captures joint linear dynamics but does not identify structural causal shocks without additional assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Treating any VAR innovation as a uniquely identified real-world intervention.
cards.prompt: What is Vector Autoregression? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Each series depends on lagged values of the vector.
Reduced-form dynamics do not alone identify causation.

cards.definition: An impulse response describes a model's future response to a specified shock. Its meaning depends on the shock definition and identification assumptions; correlated reduced-form innovations do not automatically give unique structural responses.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a multivariate model has one assumption-free causal shock decomposition.
cards.prompt: What is Impulse Response? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Dynamic response to a specified innovation or shock.
Shock identification matters.

cards.definition: X is Granger-noncausal for Y relative to a stated information set and prediction criterion if adding the past of X to the other available histories does not improve prediction of future Y. In a conditional-mean version, E[Y_(t+1)|past Y, past X, other history]=E[Y_(t+1)|past Y, other history]. A full-distribution version requires equality of the corresponding conditional laws; a linear version compares linear predictors. The convention must be declared. This predictive absence does not by itself establish absence of every intervention effect.
major_error_concepts: X is Granger-noncausal for Y precisely when the past of X improves predictions of Y after conditioning on the other available history.
cards.prompt: Define Granger-noncausality, specifying the information set and prediction convention.
required_concepts: Past X adds no predictive improvement given the retained information set.
Declare the mean, linear-prediction, or full-conditional-law convention used.
Do not equate the predictive statement with a universal intervention claim.

accepted_variants: A stationary equilibrium error between I(1) variables.
cards.definition: Cointegration occurs when nonstationary series of a given integration order have a nontrivial linear combination of lower order, commonly stationary combinations of I(1) series. It represents a shared long-run relation rather than stationarity of every level series.
major_error_concepts: Calling any highly correlated stationary pair cointegrated without an integration-order argument.
cards.prompt: What is Cointegration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Lower-order linear combination of integrated series.

cards.definition: An error-correction model combines short-run changes with adjustment to a lagged long-run equilibrium deviation. In cointegrated systems, that deviation can be stationary even though the component levels are not.
major_error_concepts: Dropping the long-run deviation while claiming to retain an error-correction term.
cards.prompt: What is Error-Correction Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Short-run differences plus lagged equilibrium error.

accepted_variants: Misleading level regression of unrelated trending series.
cards.definition: Spurious regression can show apparently strong relationships between unrelated nonstationary series because persistent trends invalidate ordinary regression reasoning. Differencing or justified cointegration modeling addresses different cases, not one universal fix.
major_error_concepts: Treating a high R-squared between random walks as sufficient evidence of a meaningful relation.
cards.prompt: What is Spurious Regression? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Nonstationary persistence can generate misleading regression evidence.

cards.definition: For a real weakly stationary process with absolutely summable autocovariance gamma(k), a spectral density in radians per sample is f(lambda)=(1/(2*pi))sum_(k in Z) gamma(k)exp(-i*k*lambda), for -pi≤lambda≤pi. The inverse is gamma(k)=integral_(-pi)^pi exp(i*k*lambda)f(lambda)d lambda; in particular variance gamma(0)=integral f. Absolute summability is sufficient, not necessary. General stationary processes have a spectral measure that need not possess a density. Other frequency conventions are valid with consistent normalization.
major_error_concepts: Using radians on [-pi,pi], white noise with variance sigma^2 has f(lambda)=sigma^2 and variance equal to integral_(-pi)^pi f(lambda)d lambda.
cards.prompt: State a spectral-density/autocovariance Fourier pair under a sufficient summability condition, declaring frequency units.
required_concepts: Give a correct Fourier/autocovariance pair in a declared frequency convention.
State a sufficient density-existence condition without claiming it is necessary.
The integral of the density over one frequency period recovers variance.

cards.definition: Frequency counts oscillations per unit time, while period is the duration per oscillation. For nonzero frequency in cycles per time, period equals the reciprocal frequency; angular frequency adds a factor of two pi.
major_error_concepts: Mixing radians per time and cycles per time without the two-pi conversion.
cards.prompt: What is Frequency and Period? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Period is reciprocal of cycle frequency.
Distinguish angular from cycle frequency.

cards.definition: A periodogram measures squared Fourier-transform magnitude at frequencies of an observed series with a stated normalization. It is a noisy finite-sample spectral estimate and generally needs smoothing or averaging for stable density estimation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a raw periodogram is automatically a consistent pointwise spectral-density estimator as the sample grows.
cards.prompt: What is Periodogram? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Squared Fourier amplitude as empirical spectrum.
Raw estimates remain noisy.

cards.definition: Aliasing occurs when distinct continuous-time frequencies produce indistinguishable sampled values. Sampling more slowly can fold high-frequency variation into apparently lower frequencies unless the signal is appropriately restricted or filtered.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a sampled series uniquely determines arbitrary unsampled high-frequency content.
cards.prompt: What is Aliasing? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Different underlying frequencies coincide after sampling.

accepted_variants: Nyquist limit for regularly sampled data.
cards.definition: For regular sampling interval Delta, the Nyquist frequency is 1/(2 Delta) cycles per unit time. Unique reconstruction requires additional bandlimiting and sampling assumptions; the number alone does not recover arbitrary signals.
major_error_concepts: Calling the full sampling frequency the Nyquist frequency.
cards.prompt: What is Nyquist Frequency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Half the sampling frequency.
Reconstruction requires appropriate signal assumptions.

cards.definition: Spectral leakage spreads finite-window signal energy across nearby Fourier frequencies. Tapering can reduce leakage at the cost of changes in frequency resolution and estimator variability.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a taper removes leakage with no loss or tradeoff.
cards.prompt: What is Spectral Leakage? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Finite observation windows spread spectral energy.
Tapering involves a tradeoff.

cards.definition: A linear filter transforms a series into weighted sums of its time-shifted values. Its frequency response describes how it changes amplitudes and phases of frequency components; two-sided filters may require future observations.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every centered filter can be used unchanged for real-time forecasting.
cards.prompt: What is Linear Time-Series Filter? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Weighted lagged or shifted values.
Filter timing affects real-time availability.

cards.definition: A cross-correlation measures association between one series and lagged values of another. Shared autocorrelation and common drivers can create prominent cross-correlations without a direct causal relationship.
major_error_concepts: Reading the largest cross-correlation peak as proof of causal delay.
cards.prompt: What is Cross-Correlation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Cross-series lagged correlation.
Dependence and confounding affect interpretation.

cards.definition: Conditional heteroskedasticity means the variance given past information changes over time. A process may have constant unconditional variance while its conditional variance responds to recent shocks.
major_error_concepts: Equating weak stationarity with constant conditional variance.
cards.prompt: What is Conditional Heteroskedasticity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Time-varying variance conditional on history.
Unconditional variance can still be constant.

cards.definition: An ARCH(q) model makes conditional variance depend on q lagged squared innovations. Nonnegative coefficients and a positive intercept ensure nonnegative variance in the basic specification; moment stability imposes additional conditions.
major_error_concepts: Treating an ARCH variance equation as the conditional mean equation.
cards.prompt: What is ARCH Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Variance responds to lagged squared errors.
Positivity and moment stability are distinct.

cards.definition: A standard GARCH(1,1) innovation model is epsilon_t=sqrt(h_t) z_t and h_t=omega+alpha epsilon_(t-1)^2+beta h_(t-1), with omega>0, alpha,beta≥0, and iid z_t independent of the past, E[z_t]=0 and E[z_t^2]=1. For the causal stationary finite-variance regime alpha+beta<1, Var(epsilon_t)=E[h_t]=omega/(1-alpha-beta). The conditional variance h_t can change over time while that unconditional variance is constant. The displayed finite-variance formula cannot be used outside its regime.
major_error_concepts: When omega=1, alpha=0.8 and beta=0.4, the stationary unconditional variance is 1/(1-1.2)=-5.
cards.prompt: State the standard GARCH(1,1) model and its stationary finite-variance formula, including assumptions.
required_concepts: State the conditional-variance recurrence and nonnegative coefficient restrictions.
Use standardized innovations independent of the past.
In the stationary finite-variance regime require alpha+beta<1 and give omega/(1-alpha-beta).

accepted_variants: Clusters of high and low variability.
cards.definition: Volatility clustering is the tendency for large absolute changes to follow large changes and small changes to follow small ones. Raw returns or errors can be nearly uncorrelated while their squares or magnitudes remain dependent.
major_error_concepts: Assuming zero raw autocorrelation rules out volatility dependence.
cards.prompt: What is Volatility Clustering? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Persistence in magnitude rather than necessarily sign.

cards.definition: A structural break changes a process parameter or relationship at a time boundary, such as a level, trend, or covariance shift. A model fitted across the break can mix incompatible regimes.
major_error_concepts: Assuming one fixed stationary model must apply before and after an unmodeled break.
cards.prompt: What is Structural Break? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Change in process structure or parameters.

cards.definition: An additive outlier is a localized disturbance to an observed value, whereas an innovation outlier enters the process disturbance and can propagate through model dynamics. Their effects need not look alike in later observations.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every unusual observation has only a one-period effect.
cards.prompt: What is Additive and Innovation Outliers? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Measurement spike versus propagating process shock.

cards.definition: An intervention model includes a specified event effect, such as a pulse or step, together with time-series error dynamics. Identifying a causal event effect still requires assumptions about competing changes and the counterfactual.
major_error_concepts: Claiming any before-after shift proves the event caused it.
cards.prompt: What is Time-Series Intervention Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Event indicator or response plus temporal errors.
Model inclusion alone does not establish causality.

cards.definition: Temporal aggregation combines observations over intervals, such as sums or averages from daily to monthly data. It changes the frequency, dependence, and sometimes the appropriate model, not just the number of rows.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a fitted daily lag coefficient transfers unchanged to monthly averages.
cards.prompt: What is Temporal Aggregation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Combine observations over time intervals.
Aggregation changes dynamic interpretation.

cards.definition: Back-transforming a forecast from a nonlinear transformed scale generally does not yield the mean on the original scale. For example, exponentiating a mean log forecast gives a median under a lognormal model, while the mean also depends on predictive variance.
major_error_concepts: Calling exp(E[log Y]) the unconditional or conditional mean of Y in general.
cards.prompt: What is Back-Transformation of Forecasts? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Nonlinear transformation and expectation do not commute.

cards.definition: A block bootstrap resamples contiguous stretches of a dependent series to preserve local dependence approximately. Block length must balance dependence preservation against the number of effectively resampled blocks under the method's assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Shuffling individual dependent observations and claiming serial structure is preserved.
cards.prompt: What is Block Bootstrap? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Resample blocks rather than isolated observations.
Block length is consequential.

cards.definition: An irregularly sampled series has observation gaps that vary. Treating adjacent records as equally spaced can distort autocorrelation and frequency interpretation; one must use actual times or an explicitly justified regularization scheme.
major_error_concepts: Assigning a single fixed elapsed duration to all unequal record gaps.
cards.prompt: What is Irregular Sampling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Unequal observation gaps.
Time-aware modeling or justified resampling needed.

cards.definition: A forecast distribution specifies probabilities for the future target conditional on current information, rather than only a point or interval. It can describe skewness, tails, and multiple possible outcomes that a mean alone hides.
major_error_concepts: Treating one point forecast as a complete probability distribution without an uncertainty model.
cards.prompt: What is Forecast Distribution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Full conditional probability law for future target.

cards.definition: Forecast calibration means issued probabilities align with observed outcome frequencies in an appropriate repeated-evaluation sense. Calibration should be considered with sharpness and the information or horizon conditioning relevant to the claim.
major_error_concepts: Calling an overconfident distribution calibrated because its point forecasts are accurate.
cards.prompt: What is Forecast Calibration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Probability statements agree with observed frequencies.
Calibration alone is not sharpness.

cards.definition: A seasonal adjustment estimates and removes recurring seasonal effects to expose other movements. Estimates using later observations may be revised, so real-time analysis must distinguish the vintage available then from a final revised series.
major_error_concepts: Using future-revised adjusted values in a historical forecast without acknowledging their later availability.
cards.prompt: What is Seasonal Adjustment? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Remove estimated seasonal component.
Revision timing matters for real-time use.

cards.definition: An impulse in an integrated process can have a permanent effect on its level, unlike a stable mean-reverting process whose response decays. Persistence refers to the response under a specified model, not simply a visually smooth plot.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all stochastic shocks eventually vanish in a random walk's level.
cards.prompt: What is Shock Persistence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Unit-root shocks need not decay in levels.
Stable dynamics and integration differ.

cards.definition: Forecast documentation records the target definition, data vintage, origin, horizon, inputs, model version, and uncertainty output. These details make an issued forecast distinguishable from a retrospective fit using later information.
major_error_concepts: Presenting an in-sample retrospective fit as an issued forecast without its information cutoff.
cards.prompt: What is Forecast Specification? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Record timing, target, data vintage, and model assumptions.

deck.title: Time Series Analysis
